findings.claim: 'the examiner is looking for causal links between events, not a list of dates'
findings.truth: The demand for an analytical narrative is real, but no examiner statement supports the framing. Reworded as advice.

findings.claim: Source B: 'a private letter sent by Georges Clemenceau to a French general in February 1919, drawn from the records of the French Foreign Ministry.'
findings.truth: The archival attribution is invented. Clause removed; see F51.
findings.evidence: no such document is in the French Foreign Ministry records

findings.claim: Nine questions across lessons 1-7, 11 and 14 are set as a '16 marks — Source-Based Essay': the stem prints two or three sources and asks the student to 'evaluate the claim' using them. Two of the sets use modern historians as sources (a 1989 article attributed to Frank McDonough, and A.J.P. Taylor described as a '1961 academic article in The Origins of the Second World War', which is a book).
findings.truth: The 16-mark question in this section is a knowledge essay on a quoted statement ('...How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.') and no sources are supplied for it; it is also the question that carries the paper's 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks. The section's source questions test contemporary sources, so a modern historian is not a source here at all. All nine retyped to '16 marks — How Far Do You Agree', the source blocks removed and the mark schemes rebuilt as support/challenge/judgement with a SPaG line.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (Paper 1, four compulsory questions worth 40 marks plus 4 SPaG marks) and AO3 'sources contemporary to the period'

findings.claim: Fifteen questions are labelled '8 marks — Source Evaluation'. Seven (lessons 1-7) print a single Source F and ask 'identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying...'. Seven more (lessons 8-10, 12-14) carry that label with no source at all. One (lesson 11) points at 'Source B above', which sits inside a different question and is never shown beside it.
findings.truth: There is no 8-mark source question on this paper. The 8-mark question is the narrative account; the 8-mark single-source usefulness question belongs to the thematic study on the other paper. The single-source questions were retyped to '4 marks — Source Analysis' with a house stem; lesson 11's was rebuilt with the Chamberlain memorandum printed inside it; the source-less ones became narrative accounts, and the Taylor one became a 16-mark essay on the intentionalist/opportunist debate.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; the four Paper 1 question forms

findings.claim: Almost every source in the practice bank is composed rather than genuine: invented wording attributed to real people at real dates (Clemenceau, Foch, Balfour, Drummond, Cecil, Baldwin, Hoare, Halifax, Chamberlain, Stalin, Litvinov, Matsuoka, Masaryk, Apponyi, Orlando, Brockdorff-Rantzau, Tabouis, Dawson, Phipps, Hankey), plus invented newspaper editorials and Punch captions.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. (1) Treat the bank as house-composed practice material and label it as such, for example 'a source composed for practice, based on X's position at the time', which is honest and cheap. (2) Rebuild the source questions on genuine out-of-copyright extracts, which exist in quantity for 1918-39 (Versailles articles, the Fourteen Points, Hitler's Reichstag speeches, the Munich Agreement, Chamberlain's Birmingham speech, the Nazi-Soviet Pact text, Haile Selassie's Geneva speech) - several are already used correctly in this unit. Recommendation: option 1 now, option 2 for the four-mark and twelve-mark questions when the bank is next touched. In the meantime the fourteen false archive attributions have been removed (see F2, F5, F10, F20, F24, F29, F31, F32, F34, F38, F41) because those are checkable claims that a teacher could try to verify.
findings.evidence: check prompt priority 6; the sources name real archives (the Wilson Papers, the Foch Papers, the Stresemann Papers, the Chamberlain Papers, the National Archives at Kew, the Beneš archive) that do not hold these documents
findings.ruling: Composed practice sources across the unit: recorded for a source-bank rebuild on genuine out-of-copyright extracts; not surgical (84 questions).

findings.claim: 'Germany lost about 13% of its European territory and 12% of its population' (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: Germany lost 65,000 km2 and about 7 million people; against a pre-war population of roughly 65 million that is about 10%, not 12%. The 13% territory figure is standard. Left alone because 12% is a common textbook figure and the error is small.

findings.claim: 'The Rhineland ... was permanently demilitarised, with no German troops or fortifications allowed within 50km of the Rhine.'
findings.truth: Versailles demilitarised the whole left bank of the Rhine plus a strip 50km east of it, not a 50km band on both sides. Corrected.

findings.claim: Source B 'drawn from German Foreign Office archives'; Source C 'drawn from the Foch Papers held at the Service Historique de la Défense, Paris'.
findings.truth: Both archival attributions are invented. Clauses removed. Foch's 'an armistice for twenty years' is genuine as a remark, but it was not a private letter with this wording; see F51.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: '16 June 1919: an ultimatum demanded German signature within seven days or fighting would resume.'
findings.truth: The Allied reply of 16 June gave five days, extended by 48 hours; a final 24-hour ultimatum followed on 23 June. Seven days is the net elapsed time, not the term of the ultimatum. Left as a note.
findings.evidence: signing of the Treaty of Versailles, June 1919

findings.claim: 'Pre-war British and French promises (the secret 1915 Treaty of London) had drawn Italy into the war.'
findings.truth: The Treaty of London was signed in April 1915, during the war, and by Britain, France and Russia. Corrected.

findings.claim: 'Japan ... was offended when Wilson rejected its proposed clause on racial equality.'
findings.truth: The amendment won a majority of the League commission's votes; Wilson, in the chair, ruled it not adopted for want of unanimity, under British and Australian pressure. Attributing the rejection to Wilson alone is misleading. Attribution removed.
findings.evidence: Paris Peace Conference, racial equality proposal, 11 April 1919

findings.claim: 'It produced a stable peace in Europe for over a decade.'
findings.truth: The Polish-Soviet war, the Greco-Turkish war, the Ruhr occupation and Corfu all fall inside that decade, and lesson 5 teaches several of them. Narrowed to peace between the great powers.

findings.claim: 'Answers that handle only two of the three elements are capped below the top band.'
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme claim. Reworded as advice.

findings.claim: Source C: 'a private memorandum by British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, December 1919, recently released from the Foreign Office archives.'
findings.truth: Balfour ceased to be Foreign Secretary on 23 October 1919, when Curzon succeeded him; in December 1919 he was Lord President of the Council. Date moved to September 1919 and the invented archive claim removed.

findings.claim: 'It dismantled four authoritarian empires and replaced them with mostly democratic governments.'
findings.truth: The Russian empire was destroyed by revolution rather than by the settlement, and what replaced it was a Bolshevik dictatorship; Hungary was authoritarian by 1920. Standard textbook shorthand, so left alone.

findings.claim: 'It came into force on 10 January 1920 ... and the League's headquarters opened in Geneva', with the key fact 'The League of Nations opened in Geneva on 10 January 1920' and the same claim in the takeaways.
findings.truth: The League's staff worked from London through 1919-20; the first Council met in Paris on 16 January 1920 and the headquarters moved to Geneva on 1 November 1920, the first Assembly meeting there on 15 November. The lesson's own practice answer already says this, so the body contradicted its own mark scheme. All three places corrected.

findings.claim: 'Examiners want particular powers, dates or mechanisms named.'
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded as an instruction to the student.

findings.claim: 'The Council met three times a year and in emergency sessions.'
findings.truth: The Covenant required the Council to meet at least once a year; in practice it met four or five times a year in the 1920s and settled at three sessions a year only after the 1929 reform. Too small and too contested to edit.

findings.claim: 'In 1920 their population voted to join Sweden. Both governments brought the dispute to the League.'
findings.truth: No plebiscite was held: Sweden proposed one and Finland refused. The real event is the 1919 petition signed by almost all adult islanders. Finland also disputed the League's jurisdiction, so 'both governments brought the dispute' is doubtful. Rewritten to the petition and a neutral 'the dispute was referred to the League'.

findings.claim: Source C: 'a 1924 article by an Italian journalist in the Roman newspaper Il Popolo d'Italia, edited by Mussolini.'
findings.truth: Il Popolo d'Italia was published in Milan, and Mussolini left its editorial staff in 1922 on becoming Prime Minister; his brother Arnaldo directed it thereafter. Corrected to 'the Milan newspaper ... the paper Mussolini had founded'.

findings.claim: 'examiners want a chain of cause and consequence, not a list'
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: 'The League organised a plebiscite in March 1921' in Upper Silesia.
findings.truth: The plebiscite of 20 March 1921 was run by an Inter-Allied Plebiscite Commission set up under the treaty; the League Council arbitrated the partition that October. The lesson follows the standard textbook shorthand, so it is left alone.

findings.claim: 'The International Labour Organization (ILO) secured 17 conventions on hours of work and the protection of women and children in industry' (repeated in a source).
findings.truth: The figure cannot be tied to a published count for the date given. Not worth an edit, but it should not be taught as a precise statistic.
findings.evidence: no source found for the figure

findings.claim: 'By 1924 ... France had withdrawn its troops from the Ruhr.'
findings.truth: Withdrawal began after the Dawes Plan of August 1924 and was completed in 1925. Corrected.

findings.claim: 'Stresemann, Briand and Austen Chamberlain shared the 1925 Nobel Peace Prize' - repeated in a mark scheme, in a second mark scheme and in a flashcard question and answer.
findings.truth: The 1925 Nobel Peace Prize went to Austen Chamberlain and Charles G. Dawes; Briand and Stresemann won the 1926 prize. Corrected in all four places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'List of Nobel Peace Prize laureates'

findings.claim: Source B 'drawn from the Stresemann Papers in the German Federal Archives'; Source F 'drawn from the Chamberlain Papers in Birmingham University Library'.
findings.truth: Both archival attributions are invented. Clauses removed; see F51.

findings.claim: 'Critics dismissed it from the start as ‘a kiss in the wind’.'
findings.truth: An unattributed quotation that does not match the recorded jibe - Senator James Reed called the pact 'an international kiss'. Quotation removed and replaced with plain description.
findings.evidence: US Senate debate on the Kellogg-Briand Pact

findings.claim: 'Negotiations began in early 1925 in the Swiss town of Locarno.'
findings.truth: The exchange of notes began in February 1925, but the conference met at Locarno only from 5 to 16 October. The sentence reads as though the town hosted talks all year.

findings.claim: 'by 1932, one in three German workers, one in four British workers and one in five French workers had no job.'
findings.truth: French unemployment peaked under 5% during the Depression; France was hit later and far less hard than Germany, Britain or the USA. The German and British figures stand. The French claim is out by a factor of four and has been removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Great Depression in France' ('unemployment peaked under 5%')

findings.claim: Source C: a Hoare memorandum 'drawn from the National Archives at Kew'.
findings.truth: Invented archival attribution. Clause removed; see F51.

findings.claim: 'For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on the League's collapse ... Examiners advise students to begin evaluating sources directly. Each source must receive a substantiated judgement on its usefulness.'
findings.truth: Wrong on the format (the 16-mark question supplies no sources) and carries an invented examiner claim. Rewritten to describe the knowledge essay and to state the 4 SPaG marks that do attach to it.

findings.claim: 'International trade collapsed by around 65% between 1929 and 1932.'
findings.truth: World trade fell by roughly two-thirds in value, but over 1929-34 rather than 1929-32, and by far less in volume. Broadly defensible; recorded rather than edited.

findings.claim: 'Mussolini, who had personally cultivated Dollfuss as an ally and whose family was even visiting Italy at the time'
findings.truth: It was Dollfuss's wife and children who were staying with the Mussolinis at Riccione. As written, the sentence says Mussolini's own family was visiting Italy. The lesson's own practice answer states it correctly. Corrected.

findings.claim: 'examiners reward causal links between events - not chronological listing'
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: Source B: a Foreign Office memorandum 'drawn from the National Archives at Kew'.
findings.truth: Invented archival attribution. Clause removed; see F51.

findings.claim: Three questions (lessons 8, 11, 13) are labelled '8 marks — Explain a Development' and ask students to explain two aims or two reasons.
findings.truth: Not a question form on this paper. All three rebuilt as 16-mark essays, using the existing aims/reasons as the two sides of the argument.

findings.claim: 'the leaders of Britain (Ramsay MacDonald), France (Pierre Laval) and Italy (Mussolini) met at Stresa' - repeated in a flashcard.
findings.truth: France was led at Stresa by Prime Minister Pierre-Étienne Flandin; Laval attended as Foreign Minister and became Prime Minister only in June 1935. Corrected in both places.

findings.claim: The 12-mark question opens 'Study Source A above and Source B', but Source A is printed inside a different question and is never shown beside it.
findings.truth: Practice questions are shown one at a time, so the source was missing and the question was unanswerable. Source A is now printed with the question (and the invented Kew provenance on Source B removed).
findings.evidence: practice.html renders one question at a time

findings.claim: Six questions (lessons 9-14) are labelled '4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different' and ask students to explain two ways in which one event differed from another.
findings.truth: That comparison question belongs to the thematic study on the other paper, where it is worth 8 marks. It is not set on this paper at any tariff. Four were rebuilt as 16-mark essays in lessons that had none, and two as narrative accounts.

findings.claim: 'Britain and France imposed sanctions on Italy' after the invasion of Abyssinia.
findings.truth: The sanctions were League sanctions, voted by the Assembly, although Britain and France drove them. The mark scheme in the same lesson says 'League sanctions'.

findings.claim: Source B: a Baldwin Cabinet memorandum 'drawn from the National Archives at Kew'.
findings.truth: Invented archival attribution. Clause removed; see F51.

findings.claim: 'examiners reward causal links between the three episodes ... not three separate stories'
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: Source A: a Halifax diary entry 'drawn from the National Archives at Kew'.
findings.truth: Invented archival attribution (and a private diary would not be there in any case). Clause removed; see F51.

findings.claim: 'Hitler thanked him in person, declaring ‘I shall never forget this’.'
findings.truth: The message was telephoned through Prince Philip of Hesse on 11 March 1938, not delivered in person. Corrected.

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward students who present these as competing interpretations rather than picking one.' (inside content_html)
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded as instruction.

findings.claim: 'For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on Anschluss or appeasement ... Begin evaluating sources directly ... Examiners reward students who present the ‘Guilty Men’ vs revisionist debate.'
findings.truth: Same false format claim as F25 plus an invented examiner claim. Rewritten.

findings.claim: Lessons 11 and 14 carry no 12-mark two-source question; lesson 8 and lesson 9 each carry only one of the four forms twice over.
findings.truth: Not an error, but after the conversion the two lessons are the only ones without practice on the paper's biggest source question. Worth adding when the bank is next touched.

findings.claim: Source D of the 16-mark question: 'a 1989 academic article by the British historian Frank McDonough on Chamberlain'. Source D of lesson 14's: 'a 1961 academic article by the British historian A.J.P. Taylor in The Origins of the Second World War'.
findings.truth: McDonough's work on Chamberlain and appeasement dates from the later 1990s and the quotation is invented; Taylor's The Origins of the Second World War is a book, not an article, and the wording quoted is a paraphrase. Both are removed with the source blocks under F47, and the lesson 14 question that pointed at 'Source D above' has been rebuilt.
findings.evidence: F. McDonough, Neville Chamberlain, Appeasement and the British Road to War (1998); A.J.P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War (1961)

findings.claim: Source C: a Beneš memorandum 'drawn from the Beneš archive in Prague'.
findings.truth: Invented archival attribution. Clause removed; see F51.

findings.claim: 'Examiners report this confusion as a recurring error in narrative accounts.' (inside content_html)
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: 'examiners report frequent chronological confusion here'
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: Source B: a Halifax memorandum 'drawn from the National Archives at Kew'.
findings.truth: Invented archival attribution. Clause removed; see F51.

findings.claim: 'examiners reward causal links between events - not just chronological listing'
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: 'Examiners ask students to weigh responsibility ... the highest-band responses present these as competing arguments.' (inside content_html)
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward students who present the debate as competing interpretations.' (inside content_html)
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. Reworded.

findings.claim: 'For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on responsibility for war ... Begin evaluating sources directly ... examiners reward students who present Hitler, Stalin and Chamberlain as competing arguments.'
findings.truth: Same false format claim as F25 plus an invented examiner claim. Rewritten.

summary: 14 lessons checked against the spec's assessment section: Paper 1 is a two-hour exam of 84 marks, this section is four compulsory questions worth 40 marks, and the 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks sit on its 16-mark essay. The practice bank did not match it. Thirty-three of the 84 questions used forms this paper does not set: nine 16-mark 'source-based essays' (the real 16-marker supplies no sources and two sets used modern historians as sources), fifteen '8 mark source evaluations' (seven with no source at all, one pointing at a source printed in a different question), six 4-mark 'two ways similar or different' comparisons from the other paper's thematic study, and three 8-mark 'explain a development' questions. All 33 were converted to the four real forms and the mark schemes rebuilt; every lesson now practises 4, 8, 12 and 16-mark work. Fifteen invented examiner claims were removed, five of them inside content_html and three inside exam tips that taught source evaluation for a knowledge essay. Fourteen invented archive attributions (the Wilson Papers, the Foch Papers, the Stresemann and Chamberlain Papers, the National Archives at Kew, the Benes archive) were stripped. The factual fixes correct the 1925 Nobel Peace Prize (Austen Chamberlain and Dawes, not Stresemann, Briand and Chamberlain - it appears four times), the League opening in Geneva in January 1920 (it worked from London until November 1920, and the lesson's own mark scheme said so), French unemployment at 'one in five' in 1932 (it peaked under 5%), Balfour as Foreign Secretary in December 1919, Laval as France's leader at Stresa, Il Popolo d'Italia as a Roman paper edited by Mussolini, the Aaland islanders 'voting' in 1920, the Rhineland's 50km rule, the French withdrawal from the Ruhr, the 1915 Treaty of London called pre-war, and Mussolini's family said to be visiting Italy when Dollfuss was shot. One ADJUDICATE: the source bank is composed rather than genuine throughout. No lesson is clean.
